_label: Evidence archive: the approach to the Ansel Adams organisation (9 August 2008)

identified_by.content: Evidence archive: the approach to the Ansel Adams organisation (9 August 2008)

content: The earliest document held in this collection: an outbound message of 2008-08-09 to the Ansel Adams organisation, carrying eight photographs of the print, following an earlier telephone contact, and signed for the love of Art. It precedes the museum approach by two days and the auction-house approach by five, and displaces the museum letter as the earliest contemporaneous document. Held as an export from the sending mailbox, whose headers were written by a present-day platform and do not independently authenticate the 2008 date.

referred_to_by.content: A single outbound message of 2008-08-09 00:46:03 UTC, from the studio principal's then-current hotmail.com mailbox to a named representative at anseladams.com, under the subject 'Ansel Adams San Francisco', carrying eight photographs of the Ansel Adams print as attachments. The body describes the camera used as 'a whopping heavyweight, weighing in at a stellar 1.3 megapixels', offers the photographs as something that 'may be of some assistance to you', gives a telephone number 'again' and invites a call in preference to email, and is signed off ' For the Love of Art '. It is the earliest document held in this collection. It precedes the approach to the museum photography department by two days and the approach to the auction house by five.

What this record displaces. Until this message was produced, this collection recorded the museum letter of 2008-08-11 as its earliest contemporaneous document, and drew from that ordering the point that the first documented outreach about the print was to a museum rather than to the trade. That ordering is now wrong and has been corrected in the museum and auction-house records. The first documented outreach was to neither: it was to the organisation that bears the photographer's name. The revised sequence is 2008-08-09 to the Adams organisation, 2008-08-11 to the museum photography department, 2008-08-14 to the auction house, all within six days and all carrying photographs from the same session.

Evidence status, stated plainly. This is the first item in the collection held as a structured message rather than as a screenshot of a mail client, and it is materially better evidence than a screenshot for what the message said, whom it was addressed to, what it carried and how it was signed. It is not better evidence of when it was sent, and this record does not claim that it is. The headers were written by Exchange Online, a platform that did not exist in 2008: the Message-ID host, the Thread-Index and the X-MS-Exchange-Organization headers are all artefacts of a present-day mailbox. There is no Received chain. That absence is on its own unremarkable, since a message taken from a Sent Items folder never accumulates Received headers, but together with the modern identifiers it shows the file to be an export of the message as it now exists in a mailbox migrated from Hotmail. The Date header is therefore metadata carried along by that mailbox. It rests on the same trust as the screenshots held elsewhere in this collection, not on transit records written by an unrelated system.

It answers an open question in the museum record, and the two documents corroborate each other. The museum letter of 2008-08-11 reports that its writer is in contact with a named person at what he calls 'the Ansel Adams Musem in SanFrancisco'. The museum record notes that no institution of that name was operating in San Francisco in 2008, the Ansel Adams Center for Photography having closed in 2001, and leaves the question open, saying the writer may have meant a differently named body. This message identifies that body. It is addressed to a named representative at anseladams.com, and it is dated two days before the museum letter, which is the order the letter's own past tense requires. The misnaming is therefore resolved as a misnaming: the organisation approached was the one bearing the photographer's name, not a San Francisco museum, and the writer described it loosely. The weight of this lies in the independence of the two artefacts. The museum letter is held as a screenshot of a mail client; this message is held as an export from a mailbox. Neither was produced from the other, neither needed to mention the other, and they agree on a fact that is checkable between them. That is a stronger form of corroboration than anything either provides alone, and it is the principal reason this record exists.

One message this is not. The museum record describes a further message of 2008-08-11, sent within a minute or two of the museum letter, opening with the first name of a named individual, carrying the same subject line and the same attachment, and copied onward to a photographic-services address. This is a different message. It is dated two days earlier, carries a different subject, and attaches eight frames rather than eleven. The two should not be conflated, and the existence of the other one means the outreach of that week was broader than the three approaches this collection now documents.

What corroborates the date, and how far it reaches. Four things, none of them a transit record, and they are cumulative rather than decisive. All eight attachments are byte-identical to members of the same name in San Francisco.zip, an archive already held and already checksummed in the auction-house record, so the message and that archive are tied to each other. The attachments' EXIF DateTimeOriginal values run from 2008-08-08 00:05:33 to 00:10:22, one session of about five minutes on the day before the message's stated date. The EXIF camera model is FUJIFILM FinePix1300, which agrees with the body's own description of a 1.3 megapixel camera, a detail the writer had no reason to plant. And the body carries a Windows Live Hotmail promotional footer of the period. Taken together these make the stated date coherent with independent artefacts; they do not make it independently attested. A copy retained by the receiving organisation would. None has been sought.

The message is a follow-up, not a first approach. Two phrases establish this. The writer says 'I hope this may be of some assistance to you', which presumes a request or an interest already expressed, and he gives his telephone number 'again', which presumes he has given it before. So contact with the Adams organisation began before 2008-08-09, and it began by telephone. Nothing of that earlier contact is held: no note, no call record, no reply. The earliest document in this collection is therefore not the beginning of the engagement it documents, and no claim about a first approach should rest on it.

The subject line, and what is not yet in it. This message is headed 'Ansel Adams San Francisco'. The messages of 2008-08-11 and 2008-08-14, to the museum and to the auction house, are headed 'Ansel Adams Finds Art in SanFrancisco', and the auction house's replies carry that subject forward. The art-inflected subject is therefore not present at the earliest date, and appears two days later. The observation is recorded and not interpreted. It is equally consistent with a framing that developed across that week and with a writer choosing a plainer heading for a plainer request; nothing held distinguishes the two.

The sign-off, moved back. The valediction ' For the Love of Art ' closes this message of 2008-08-09, and so predates by two days the earliest previously documented use of it. The auction-house record treats the phrase at length, as the studio's own adaptation of the title of Damien Hirst's For the Love of God, and observes that it closes both approaches of August 2008 and so was a settled signature rather than a one-off. That observation is strengthened here: the phrase now closes three approaches, to three different organisations, across six days. What it is not, here as there, is a reference anyone was invited to see. The studio's account of the Hirst adaptation is its own, given in 2026, and is reported as that account rather than as a fact these messages establish.

What it establishes, and what it does not. It establishes that by 2008-08-09 the studio principal held the Ansel Adams print, had photographed it the previous night, and was approaching organisations about it, beginning with the one bearing the photographer's name; that this approach followed an earlier telephone contact; and that the sign-off used throughout the August 2008 outreach was in use from its earliest documented moment. It does not touch Metaconceptual Art, which is not named in it. It does not describe the print, the photographs, or the approach as an artwork, a performance or a project of any kind: the message offers assistance and asks for a call. And it carries no designation of the auction, which had not been proposed to anyone when it was written.

Redaction and scope. Following this collection's convention, the representative at the Adams organisation, who was addressed in an official capacity, is identified by role only; their given name and mailbox are withheld pending consent and retained in the studio's private copy. Both correspondents' mailbox addresses are replaced, and the studio principal's telephone number is withheld as personal data, though the fact that the message gives a number, and gives it 'again', is preserved because it is what evidences the prior contact. The domain anseladams.com is deliberately retained: the identity of the organisation approached is the point of the record. No endorsement by that organisation of this project, of Metaconceptual Art, or of any claim in this collection is implied or should be inferred. It has not been approached about this message and has said nothing about it. The unredacted original is not published; its SHA-256 is, so that the held file can later be shown to be unaltered without its contents being disclosed.
